cards.question: What should you establish first in an AI system design interview?
options: The model architecture and embedding dimensions
Requirements: the user problem, success metric, scale, latency budget, and constraints, before proposing any architecture
Which vector database and cloud provider to use
The training data volume needed
cards.explanation: Jumping to architecture is the most common failure, because the right design depends entirely on constraints you haven't established. Clarify what decision or action the system supports, how success is measured, expected traffic and growth, latency requirements, budget, data availability and sensitivity, and what happens when the system is wrong. That last question often reshapes the design more than anything else, since a system where errors are cheap and reversible can be far more aggressive than one where they aren't. Stating assumptions explicitly and confirming them is also what lets an interviewer redirect you early rather than watch you design the wrong thing.
cards.modelAnswer: Requirements, explicitly, before any architecture. I'd ask what user problem this solves and what decision or action it drives, because that determines the metric. Then how success is measured in business terms, not just model terms. Then the operating envelope: expected traffic now and in a year, latency budget, and cost constraints. Then data: what exists, how it's labeled, how sensitive it is, and whether it can leave our environment. And crucially, what happens when the system is wrong, since a recommendation with a cheap reversible error tolerates a much more aggressive design than an automated decision affecting someone's account or health. I'd state my assumptions out loud as I go so the interviewer can correct me early rather than letting me build the wrong thing for twenty minutes, and I'd sketch the simplest architecture that satisfies the requirements before adding sophistication, since justifying complexity against a stated requirement is the actual skill being tested.

cards.question: In a two-stage recommender, why separate candidate generation from ranking?
options: To allow different teams to own each stage
Because you can't afford an expensive model over millions of items, so a cheap recall-oriented stage narrows to hundreds that a rich precision-oriented model can score
Because candidate generation requires a GPU and ranking does not
To avoid overfitting in the ranking model
cards.explanation: Scoring every item with a heavy feature-rich model is computationally impossible at catalog scale within a latency budget. So retrieval optimizes recall cheaply, typically with ANN search over embeddings plus heuristic sources like popularity and recent interactions, reducing millions to hundreds. Ranking then spends real compute per item, using cross features, user history, and context to optimize precision at the top. Many systems add a third re-ranking stage for business logic: diversity, freshness, deduplication, promotions, and fairness constraints. The key insight is that each stage has a different objective, so recall failures at stage one are unrecoverable, which is why retrieval usually combines multiple sources.
cards.modelAnswer: It's a compute-versus-quality decomposition forced by scale. You cannot score ten million items with a feature-rich model inside a hundred-millisecond budget, but you also can't get good recommendations from a model cheap enough to run over everything. So stage one optimizes recall cheaply, usually approximate nearest neighbor search over user and item embeddings, often unioned with heuristic sources like trending, recently viewed, and same-category items, taking millions down to a few hundred. Stage two spends real compute per candidate, using rich cross features, sequence models over user history, and context to optimize precision at the very top of the list, since that's all the user sees. A lot of systems add a third stage for business logic that isn't naturally expressed in a relevance score: diversity so the list isn't ten near-identical items, freshness, deduplication, promotional boosts, and any fairness or supply constraints. The asymmetry worth naming is that a recall miss at stage one is unrecoverable, since ranking can only reorder what it's given, which is exactly why retrieval blends multiple sources rather than relying on one embedding space.

cards.question: How do you handle the cold-start problem for new users and items?
options: Wait until enough interaction data accumulates
Fall back to content-based signals and metadata, use popularity or contextual defaults, and explore deliberately to gather signal
Train a separate model exclusively for new users
Assign new users the average of all existing user embeddings
cards.explanation: Pure collaborative filtering fails with no interactions, so you need signals that don't require history. For new items, use content features: text, images, category, and creator, embedded into the same space so they're retrievable immediately. For new users, use context (locale, device, referrer, time), any onboarding preferences, and popularity priors, then update rapidly as the first interactions arrive, since early sessions are highly informative. Deliberate exploration matters too, because a purely exploitative system never shows new items, so they never get impressions, so they never accumulate data, which is a self-reinforcing failure that also starves your catalog. Hybrid models that combine collaborative and content signals degrade gracefully instead of having a hard cold-start boundary.
cards.modelAnswer: The root issue is that collaborative signals require history, so I'd lean on signals that don't. For a new item, content-based features carry it: title, description, images, category, creator, embedded into the same space as everything else so it's retrievable from the moment it's created rather than after its hundredth interaction. For a new user, context is surprisingly strong, locale, device, referral source, and time of day, plus anything captured in onboarding, with popularity priors as the floor. Then I'd update aggressively during the first session, because early interactions are enormously informative relative to later ones, which argues for a fast online update path rather than waiting for a nightly retrain. The part people miss is exploration. A purely exploitative ranker never surfaces new items, so they get no impressions, so they never accumulate the data that would let them rank, which is a self-reinforcing trap that quietly starves your catalog and hurts supply-side retention. So I'd reserve some slots for exploration, either an explicit epsilon or a bandit approach that treats uncertainty as a reason to show something. Architecturally I'd prefer a hybrid model that consumes both collaborative and content features, since it degrades gradually as history thins rather than having a hard cliff.

cards.question: For a content moderation system, why is the threshold choice as important as the model?
options: Because thresholds affect inference latency
Because it sets the precision-recall tradeoff, which determines the balance of harmful content missed versus legitimate content wrongly removed
Because thresholds must be recalibrated for each language
Because a single threshold makes the model deterministic
cards.explanation: The model produces a score; the threshold turns it into an action, and that's where the policy tradeoff lives. A low threshold catches more violations but removes more legitimate content, which is a real harm to users and to trust; a high threshold does the reverse. The right answer is usually not a single threshold but tiered actions: auto-remove above a high-confidence band, route a middle band to human review, and allow below it, with the bands set by review capacity and the severity of the category. Severity should drive the tradeoff, so child safety or imminent-harm categories warrant much higher recall than spam. Thresholds also need per-category and per-language calibration and periodic revisiting as adversaries adapt.
cards.modelAnswer: The model outputs a score, but the threshold is what converts it into an action, and that conversion is a policy decision with real costs on both sides: false negatives leave harmful content up, false positives remove legitimate speech and erode user trust, and both are genuine harms rather than one being merely an inconvenience. So it can't be set by maximizing F1 in a notebook. What I'd actually build is tiered rather than binary: above a high-confidence band, auto-action; a middle uncertainty band routed to human review; below that, allow, possibly with monitoring. That structure lets me tune the review band to my actual human review capacity, which is the real operational constraint. Then thresholds should vary by severity, so a category like child safety or credible threats warrants far higher recall even at heavy precision cost, while spam can tolerate misses. And they need per-category and per-language calibration, because a single global threshold will be far too aggressive in some languages and too lax in others given uneven training data. Finally I'd revisit them regularly, since adversaries adapt specifically to whatever boundary you deploy.

cards.question: What are the main components of a semantic search system?
options: A crawler and an inverted index
Ingestion and chunking, an embedding model, a vector index with metadata, a query path with optional rewriting and reranking, and evaluation plus monitoring
A large language model with a long context window
A relational database with full-text search enabled
cards.explanation: Offline: crawl or ingest documents, parse and chunk them, embed, and index vectors alongside filterable metadata and the original text. Online: process the query (normalization, possibly rewriting or expansion), retrieve candidates via vector and usually lexical search, fuse and rerank, then return results with snippets. Around both: an evaluation harness with labeled query-document relevance, monitoring of latency, recall proxies, zero-result rates, and click signals, plus a reindexing path for when the embedding model changes. Most production systems are hybrid rather than purely semantic, since exact-match needs like names, codes, and identifiers don't survive embedding alone.
cards.modelAnswer: There's an offline indexing path and an online query path, plus the evaluation and operational layer that people forget to mention. Offline: ingest documents from their sources, parse them structurally, chunk into retrievable units, embed each chunk, and write vectors plus filterable metadata plus the original text into an index. Online: normalize and optionally rewrite the query, retrieve candidates with both vector and lexical search, fuse the lists, rerank with a cross-encoder if latency allows, and return results with highlighted snippets. Around that: an evaluation harness with labeled query-relevance pairs so I can measure recall and nDCG rather than guessing, monitoring for latency, zero-result rate, and click-through as a live quality proxy, and a reindexing path for the day the embedding model changes, which is a real operational event at scale. I'd emphasize that production semantic search is almost always hybrid rather than purely dense, because exact-match needs, product codes, people's names, error identifiers, don't survive embedding, and a system that can't find an SKU will be judged broken regardless of how good its paraphrase matching is.

cards.question: How would you design a real-time fraud detection system?
options: Batch score transactions nightly and flag suspicious ones for review
Score synchronously in the payment path with strict latency limits, combining streaming features, a model, and rules, with tiered actions and a feedback loop for delayed labels
Use an LLM to reason about each transaction in natural language
Block all transactions above a fixed amount threshold
cards.explanation: Fraud must be decided before the transaction completes, so the model sits in the synchronous path with a tight budget (often tens of milliseconds) and must fail open or degrade to rules rather than block payments if it's unavailable. Features come from a streaming layer computing velocity and aggregate signals (transactions per card per hour, device and IP history, geo-velocity) with point-in-time correctness so training doesn't leak future information. Actions are tiered: allow, challenge with step-up authentication, hold for review, or decline, since a challenge is a far cheaper intervention than a false decline. Design constraints that matter: extreme class imbalance, so evaluate with PR-AUC and cost-weighted metrics; adversarial drift, since fraudsters adapt to your boundary, requiring frequent retraining and rules for fast response to new patterns; delayed and biased labels, since chargebacks arrive weeks later and declined transactions never generate outcomes; and the business tradeoff that a false decline costs a good customer while a missed fraud costs the chargeback, with the ratio set by the business, not the modeler.
cards.modelAnswer: The defining constraint is that the decision has to happen inside the payment authorization path, so I'm designing a synchronous service with a budget of maybe tens of milliseconds that must degrade gracefully, falling back to rules rather than failing payments if the model is unavailable. Features come from a streaming aggregation layer, since the strongest fraud signals are velocity and relational: transactions per card per hour, distinct merchants per device, geo-velocity between consecutive transactions, whether this device or IP has been seen with other accounts. Those need point-in-time correctness in training, or I'll leak future information and dramatically overestimate offline performance. On the decision, I'd avoid a binary allow-or-decline and use tiered actions: allow, step-up challenge, hold for manual review, decline. That matters because a challenge costs a little friction while a false decline costs a good customer's trust and possibly their business, so having a middle option changes the economics substantially. Then the properties that make fraud distinctive. Extreme imbalance, so I'd evaluate with PR-AUC and cost-weighted metrics rather than accuracy, and set the threshold from the actual dollar ratio between a chargeback and a lost customer. Adversarial drift, since fraudsters probe and adapt to whatever boundary I deploy, which means frequent retraining plus a fast rules layer so analysts can respond to a new pattern in hours rather than waiting for a model cycle. And label problems: chargebacks arrive weeks later so feedback is delayed, and declined transactions never produce an outcome, so my training data is censored by my own past decisions, which argues for holding out a small randomized allow slice to keep the measurement honest. I'd also plan for analyst tooling and explanations from day one, since a score with no reason codes is unusable for review and often insufficient for regulatory obligations around adverse action.

cards.question: Design a system to detect duplicate or near-duplicate listings at scale. What's your approach?
options: Compare every pair of listings with a cross-encoder
Blocking or LSH to generate candidate pairs cheaply, then a pairwise classifier on features, with clustering to resolve transitive groups and a human review path
Exact string matching on the title field
Cluster all listings with k-means and treat each cluster as a duplicate group
cards.explanation: The core problem is that pairwise comparison is quadratic, so you can't score all pairs. The standard entity-resolution pipeline is candidate generation followed by scoring: use blocking on cheap keys (category plus location, normalized title tokens) or MinHash/SimHash LSH for text and perceptual hashing for images to produce a manageable candidate set with high recall. Then score candidates with a classifier over similarity features (text and image embedding similarity, price delta, seller identity, geo distance) or a cross-encoder, which is affordable now that the set is small. Then resolve transitivity, since duplicate relations form clusters and A~B plus B~C implies a group, typically with connected components or correlation clustering, being careful that loose thresholds cause runaway merged clusters. Finally, decide actions by confidence, auto-merging only high-confidence pairs and routing the rest to review, since wrongly merging two distinct listings is usually worse than missing a duplicate.
cards.modelAnswer: The fundamental constraint is quadratic pair growth, so the design is candidate generation followed by expensive scoring, exactly like retrieval and ranking. For candidates I'd use blocking on cheap high-precision keys where the domain allows, category plus geography, or normalized title tokens, combined with MinHash or SimHash LSH for text near-duplication and perceptual hashing for images, since image reuse is often the strongest duplicate signal in listings. The goal at this stage is recall with a manageable candidate count, and I'd measure that explicitly, because a blocking scheme that silently drops true duplicates caps the whole system. Then a pairwise scorer over engineered similarity features, text and image embedding similarity, price difference, seller identity, posting time proximity, geographic distance, plus a cross-encoder on titles and descriptions if latency allows, since it's affordable once the candidate set is small. The step people forget is transitivity resolution: duplicate is effectively an equivalence relation, so if A matches B and B matches C they belong in one group, which means running connected components or correlation clustering over the match graph. I'd flag the failure mode there, that a slightly loose threshold causes runaway merges where thousands of listings collapse into one cluster through chains of weak links, so I'd cap cluster size and use stricter thresholds for merging than for flagging. Finally, action by confidence: auto-merge only very high confidence, route the middle to human review, and treat a wrong merge as more costly than a missed duplicate, since destroying a legitimate seller's listing is a worse outcome than showing a redundant one. And I'd design for incremental operation, scoring each new listing against candidates at write time rather than reprocessing the corpus.

cards.question: How would you architect an LLM-powered customer support assistant?
options: Fine-tune a model on all historical support tickets and deploy it directly
RAG over versioned help content with citations, intent routing, tool access for account lookups, abstention and human escalation, plus evaluation and guardrails
A single large model with all policies in the system prompt
A decision tree of scripted responses with an LLM for phrasing
cards.explanation: Knowledge belongs in retrieval, not weights, because support policies change weekly and answers must be citable and correctable without retraining. So: index help center, policy docs, and resolved tickets with versioning; classify intent to route (informational questions to RAG, account-specific questions to tools, high-risk topics like legal, billing disputes, or safety straight to a human); give the model narrow read tools for order and account status so it can answer specific questions rather than generic ones; and require grounded answers with citations plus abstention and escalation when retrieval is weak. Escalation must be first-class, transferring full context to an agent, because trapping a frustrated customer is the dominant failure. Add guardrails for PII, refusal boundaries on commitments the company can't honor, and injection resistance since users control the input. Then evaluation from historical tickets, per-conversation tracing, and a rollout that starts with agent-assist (drafting for human review) before customer-facing traffic.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd put knowledge in retrieval rather than weights, because support policy changes constantly and answers need to be citable and correctable without a training cycle, so I'd index the help center, policy documents, and resolved tickets with version metadata. On top of that, intent routing, because support traffic isn't homogeneous: informational questions go to RAG, account-specific questions need tool calls to look up order or subscription state, and high-risk categories, billing disputes, legal, cancellations, or anything suggesting distress, route straight to a human without the model attempting an answer. Tools would be narrow and read-only initially, scoped to the authenticated user's own records, since that's what turns generic answers into useful ones without taking on write-action risk early. Then the behavioral requirements: answers grounded with citations, explicit abstention when retrieval is weak, and escalation as a first-class path that transfers the full conversation context to an agent, plus an always-available route to a human, because trapping a frustrated customer in a loop is the failure that generates real damage and it's a product decision rather than a model one. Guardrails: PII redaction in logs, refusal boundaries so the model never commits to refunds, exceptions, or legal positions without policy backing, and injection resistance since the user controls the input. For evaluation I'd build the set from historical tickets, covering common intents, the long tail, and the specific failure classes I care about, and instrument per-conversation traces with sampled groundedness scoring. And I'd sequence the rollout to earn trust: start as agent-assist where it drafts and a human sends, which gathers labeled data at zero customer risk, then low-risk intents at small traffic share, expanding by intent as evidence accumulates.

cards.question: What are the key design decisions for a document processing pipeline (OCR to structured data)?
options: Choosing the largest available vision model
Parsing strategy per document type, layout and table handling, extraction with schema validation, confidence-based human review, and handling of multi-page and low-quality inputs
Whether to store documents as PDF or images
The number of GPUs allocated to OCR
cards.explanation: Real difficulty is in the document variety, not the model. Decisions: route by document type and quality, since a digital-text PDF should be parsed directly rather than OCR'd, while scans and photos need OCR and possibly deskewing; handle layout explicitly, because reading order in multi-column documents and preservation of table structure are the dominant sources of downstream error; extract into a defined schema with validation and type coercion, so failures are visible rather than silent; attach per-field confidence and route low-confidence fields to human review rather than the whole document, which is far cheaper; and handle multi-page context where a value on page 12 refers to a header on page 1. Also plan for evaluation with field-level accuracy on a labeled set stratified by document type and quality, since aggregate accuracy hides the classes that break, and design the human-in-the-loop tooling as part of the system rather than an afterthought, since it's where the corrections that improve the model come from.
cards.modelAnswer: The hard part is document variety, not model choice. First decision is routing by input type, since a born-digital PDF has extractable text and OCR-ing it is both slower and worse, while scans and phone photos need OCR with deskewing and quality handling, so I'd detect and branch rather than running one path. Second, layout, which is where most downstream errors actually originate: reading order in multi-column documents, and table structure, because flattening a table destroys the row-column relationships that carry the meaning, so I'd use a layout-aware parser and keep tables as structured objects. Third, extraction into an explicit schema with validation and type coercion, so a date that doesn't parse or a total that doesn't match line items surfaces as an error rather than propagating silently into a downstream system, and I'd add cross-field consistency checks since they catch a lot. Fourth, confidence and human review, and specifically field-level rather than document-level, since routing one uncertain field to a reviewer is far cheaper than re-keying a whole invoice, and that granularity is what makes the economics work. Fifth, multi-page handling, since a value on page twelve often depends on a header or context from page one, so chunking naively per page loses it. For evaluation I'd want field-level accuracy on a labeled set stratified by document type and quality, because an aggregate number hides the specific document class that fails completely, which is exactly what a customer will send. And I'd treat the human review tooling as part of the system rather than an afterthought, since it's both the safety net and the source of the corrections that let me improve extraction over time.

cards.question: How do you design for multi-tenancy in an AI application?
options: One shared model and one shared index, with tenant filtering in the prompt
Isolate tenant data at the storage and query layer, with per-tenant quotas, cost attribution, and a documented isolation model appropriate to the risk
A separate full deployment per tenant, always
Rely on encryption to keep tenant data separate
cards.explanation: The central risk is cross-tenant data leakage, which is a security incident rather than a quality issue, so isolation must be enforced in the data path, never by prompt instruction. Choose an isolation level by risk and scale: separate indexes or namespaces per tenant give the strongest guarantees and the cleanest deletion story at higher infrastructure cost, while a shared index with mandatory tenant filters applied inside the search is cheaper but relies on those filters being impossible to bypass. Beyond data: per-tenant rate limits and spend caps, since one tenant's agent loop shouldn't exhaust capacity or budget for everyone; noisy-neighbor protection at the serving layer, since a tenant sending very long contexts consumes disproportionate KV cache memory; per-tenant cost attribution so pricing reflects usage; and per-tenant configuration and possibly adapters, served via multi-adapter LoRA rather than dedicated deployments. Also address deletion, since tenant offboarding must remove data from the vector index, caches, logs, and traces, which is easy to overlook.
cards.modelAnswer: The dominant risk is cross-tenant leakage, and I'd frame it as a security boundary rather than a relevance concern, which means enforcement lives in the data path and never in a prompt instruction, since a model can be injected or can simply ignore an instruction. Then I'd pick an isolation level from the risk profile: separate indexes or namespaces per tenant give the strongest guarantee and make offboarding a drop rather than a delete-scan, at more infrastructure cost and worse resource sharing, while a shared index with mandatory tenant predicates applied inside the ANN search is cheaper but depends on that filter being structurally impossible to omit, so I'd enforce it in a data access layer rather than trusting each call site, and I'd write adversarial tests for it. Beyond data isolation there's resource isolation, which people underestimate: per-tenant rate limits and spend caps so one tenant's runaway agent loop doesn't exhaust capacity or budget for everyone, and noisy-neighbor protection at the serving layer, since a tenant submitting very long contexts consumes disproportionate KV cache memory and can degrade latency for all sequences on that node. I'd want per-tenant cost attribution from day one, because otherwise pricing and margin analysis become guesswork and you can't identify an unprofitable customer. For customization, per-tenant configuration and prompts first, and if per-tenant models are genuinely needed, LoRA adapters over a shared base with multi-adapter serving rather than dedicated deployments. And I'd design deletion explicitly, since offboarding has to remove data from the vector index, caches, logs, and observability traces, and that last one is routinely missed until a compliance review finds it.

cards.question: How would you design an AI coding assistant's context retrieval?
options: Embed every file and retrieve by similarity to the user's question
Combine structural signals (open files, cursor location, imports, call graph, recent edits) with retrieval, respecting a token budget and repository conventions
Include the entire repository in the context window
Retrieve only files whose names match keywords in the query
cards.explanation: Code has structure that pure embedding similarity ignores, and that structure is more informative than semantic similarity for most requests. Strong signals: the currently open file and cursor position, the file's imports and type definitions, symbols referenced at the cursor resolved through the call graph or language server, recently edited files, and the current diff or branch. Retrieval still helps for finding similar patterns and usages elsewhere, and it should chunk on syntactic boundaries (functions, classes) rather than fixed line counts so chunks are meaningful. Then budget the context deliberately: signatures and type definitions often matter more per token than full implementations, so summarize or elide bodies. Also include project conventions such as lint config, test patterns, and neighboring code style, since matching the codebase's idiom is a large part of perceived quality, and keep permissions in mind for private code.
cards.modelAnswer: The key insight is that code has explicit structure, and that structure beats embedding similarity for most requests. So I'd start with structural signals: the open file and cursor position, which tells me what the user is actually working on, the file's imports and the type definitions they resolve to, symbols referenced near the cursor resolved through a language server or call graph so I include actual definitions rather than something that merely looks similar, recently edited files, and the current diff or branch, since a feature in progress is highly indicative of intent. Embedding retrieval is still valuable but for a different job: finding similar patterns and existing usages elsewhere in the repo, which is how you get code that matches how this team already does things. For that I'd chunk on syntactic boundaries, functions and classes via a parser, rather than fixed line windows, since a chunk cut mid-function is nearly useless. Then I'd treat the token budget as a real allocation problem, because value per token varies enormously: function signatures and type definitions are often more useful than full bodies, so eliding implementations while keeping interfaces buys a lot of coverage. And I'd include project conventions, lint and formatter config, test file patterns, and neighboring code style, since a suggestion that's functionally right but idiomatically foreign gets rejected, and matching the codebase's idiom is a large share of perceived quality. Two practical constraints: latency budget is tight for inline completion so the retrieval has to be fast and mostly local, and for private repositories I'd be careful about what leaves the machine and what's retained.

cards.question: What's the right architecture for a system that must answer both structured and unstructured questions?
options: Embed the database rows as text and use one vector index for everything
Route by query type: text-to-SQL over the warehouse for analytical questions, RAG for prose, with a router and a path that combines both when needed
Always use SQL, generating it from natural language for every question
Always use RAG, since it handles any content type
cards.explanation: Embedding aggregation away doesn't work: no chunk contains 'total revenue by region last quarter' because that's a computation, and flattening rows to text loses the relational structure. So classify the query and route it. Structured analytical questions go to text-to-SQL, which needs schema retrieval (real warehouses have far too many columns for the context window), column descriptions, enum values, and verified example queries, with execution through a read-only role with row limits and timeouts, and results narrated by the model rather than invented. Prose questions go to RAG. Some questions need both, for example a policy explanation plus the user's own numbers, so the orchestration layer must support combining results. Evaluate the SQL path with execution accuracy against gold result sets rather than string similarity, and surface the generated query to the user for transparency, since a wrong number presented confidently is worse than a visible query they can sanity-check.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd route rather than force one mechanism, because the two question types need fundamentally different machinery. Embedding a database doesn't work for analytical questions: aggregation, filtering, and joins are computations, so no chunk contains total revenue by region last quarter, and flattening rows into text destroys the relational structure that makes the data useful. So a router classifies the query and dispatches. Analytical questions go down a text-to-SQL path, where the interesting engineering is schema retrieval, since a real warehouse has thousands of columns and can't fit in context, so I retrieve the relevant tables and columns plus their descriptions, enum values, and a set of verified example queries, which in my experience is the single highest-leverage input to SQL accuracy. Generated SQL is then treated as untrusted: executed via a read-only role with row limits and a timeout, and I'd surface the query to the user, because a visible query they can sanity-check is far safer than a confident number with no provenance. The model narrates the returned rows rather than producing numbers itself, which is what keeps it grounded. Prose questions go to RAG as usual. And I'd make sure the orchestration layer can combine both, since real questions like why did my bill increase need the policy document and the customer's actual charges together. For evaluation I'd use execution accuracy on the SQL path, comparing result sets against gold queries rather than comparing SQL strings, since many different queries are correct. And I'd handle the ambiguity case explicitly: when the router isn't confident, asking a clarifying question is better than guessing, because a confidently wrong analytical answer is the failure mode that destroys trust in these systems.

cards.question: How do you design an ML system when labeled data is scarce?
options: Wait until enough labels are collected before building anything
Start with heuristics or a pretrained/zero-shot model, then use active learning, weak supervision, and targeted labeling to bootstrap while shipping value
Use unsupervised learning exclusively
Generate all labels synthetically with an LLM and treat them as ground truth
cards.explanation: Ship something useful first, then bootstrap. A rules baseline or a zero/few-shot LLM often clears the initial bar and, importantly, starts generating the traffic and feedback that produce labels. Then invest labeling effort where it pays: active learning selects the most informative examples, typically high-uncertainty or high-disagreement cases, so a few hundred labels go much further than random sampling. Weak supervision (labeling functions over heuristics, keywords, or existing metadata, combined probabilistically) can produce large noisy training sets cheaply. Transfer learning and LLM-based labeling with human verification of a sample also work well, provided you validate the labeler's agreement with humans rather than assuming it. Throughout, guard the evaluation set: it must be human-labeled and trustworthy even when training labels are noisy, since otherwise you can't tell whether anything is improving.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd ship something useful immediately rather than blocking on labels, because a system in production is what generates the feedback that produces labels. That usually means a heuristic baseline or a zero-shot or few-shot LLM, which for many classification and extraction tasks clears the initial bar surprisingly well and gives me a real measurement of task difficulty. Then I'd bootstrap deliberately. Active learning to make labeling budget go further: rather than labeling randomly, label the examples the model is most uncertain about or where an ensemble disagrees, which typically gets you the same performance for a fraction of the annotations. Weak supervision where the domain permits it, writing labeling functions from heuristics, keywords, and existing metadata and combining them probabilistically to produce a large noisy training set, which is often enough to train a decent first model. Transfer learning so I'm adapting a pretrained representation rather than learning from scratch, since that's what makes a few hundred examples viable at all. And LLM-based labeling, which is genuinely effective now, but with a sampled human verification loop, because if I don't measure the labeler's agreement with humans I'm just training on its assumptions. The one thing I'd protect absolutely is the evaluation set: it has to be human-labeled and trustworthy even while training labels are noisy, because if both training and evaluation come from the same automated source I've lost the ability to tell whether anything is actually improving, and that's the mistake that lets a project run for months in the wrong direction.

cards.question: Design a system that routes requests between a small and a large model. What are the hard parts?
options: Choosing the two models; the routing itself is a simple length threshold
Predicting difficulty before generating, calibrating the escalation threshold against cost and quality, and handling the router's own errors and drift
Running both models on every request and picking the better answer
Routing by user tier, since paying users deserve the larger model
cards.explanation: The premise is sound, since most traffic is easy and a small model handles it at a fraction of the cost, but the difficulty is that you must decide before you have the answer. Options: a learned classifier on the query (cheap, needs training data from labeled easy/hard examples); the small model's own confidence or self-assessment, which is often poorly calibrated; or cascade with verification, where the small model answers, a cheap verifier checks it, and only failures escalate, which is more reliable but adds latency to the escalated path. Hard parts beyond that: calibrating the threshold, since the cost curve and the quality curve move in opposite directions and the right point depends on the value of a correct answer; router errors are asymmetric, because wrongly routing a hard query to the small model produces a bad answer while the reverse merely costs money, so the threshold should be conservative; latency variance becomes bimodal, complicating SLOs; the router needs its own monitoring and retraining as traffic and models change; and evaluation must cover the routed system end to end rather than each model separately.
cards.modelAnswer: The economics are compelling, since most production traffic is easy and a small model handles it at a fraction of the cost, but the core difficulty is that routing requires predicting difficulty before you have an answer to judge. Three approaches with different tradeoffs. A learned classifier over the query is cheapest and adds negligible latency, but it needs training data, meaning labeled examples of what the small model gets right and wrong, which you have to generate deliberately. Using the small model's own confidence is appealing but LLM self-assessed confidence is poorly calibrated, so I'd be skeptical without measuring it. Cascade with verification is the most reliable: the small model answers, a cheap verifier or the small model itself checks the answer, and only failures escalate, which trades latency on the escalated path for much better routing accuracy. Then the genuinely hard parts. Threshold calibration, because the cost curve and quality curve move opposite each other and the right operating point depends on what a correct answer is worth, so that's a product decision I'd surface rather than pick. Asymmetric errors: sending a hard query to the small model produces a bad user-facing answer, while sending an easy one to the large model just costs money, so the threshold should lean conservative and I'd measure the two error types separately rather than as one accuracy number. Latency becomes bimodal, which complicates SLOs and makes p95 behave unintuitively. The router is itself a model that drifts, so it needs monitoring and retraining as traffic patterns and the underlying models change, and a model upgrade can silently invalidate its learned boundary. And evaluation must be end to end on the routed system, since measuring each model separately tells you nothing about the composite behavior users actually get.

cards.question: How would you design a multi-agent system, and when is it actually the right choice?
options: Always use multiple agents, since specialization improves quality
Only when work is genuinely parallel or requires isolated context; otherwise a single agent with good tools is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug
Use one agent per tool, coordinated by a central planner
Multi-agent systems are always preferable for long tasks
cards.explanation: Multi-agent designs are frequently over-applied. Each handoff loses context, error rates compound across steps, cost multiplies, latency grows, and debugging becomes much harder because failures emerge from interaction rather than a single trace. A single agent with well-designed tools handles most tasks better. Multi-agent genuinely wins when subtasks are independent and can run in parallel (searching many sources at once, reviewing many files), when context isolation is valuable so one subtask's large intermediate output doesn't pollute the main context, or when a genuinely different capability, model, or permission set is needed per role. When you do build one, be explicit about orchestration: prefer a coordinator with parallel workers over free-form agent-to-agent chat, define narrow structured interfaces between agents rather than passing prose, keep shared state external and authoritative rather than replicated in each agent's context, and cap depth, iterations, and spend. Also design for partial failure, since one worker failing shouldn't silently produce a confident but incomplete result.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd start by pushing back on the premise, because multi-agent is over-applied and the costs are real: every handoff loses context, error rates compound multiplicatively across steps so five ninety-percent steps give you sixty percent, cost and latency multiply, and debugging gets much harder since failures emerge from interaction rather than appearing in one trace. A single agent with well-designed tools is more reliable, cheaper, and more debuggable for most tasks, and I'd want a specific reason to move past it. The reasons that do justify it. Genuine parallelism, where subtasks are independent, searching ten sources or reviewing twenty files simultaneously, and the wall-clock win is real rather than imagined. Context isolation, where a subtask produces a large intermediate result that would pollute the main context, so a subagent can read a hundred files and return a summary, keeping the orchestrator's context clean. And genuinely different roles, where a step needs a different model, different tools, or different permissions, for instance a reviewer that shouldn't have write access. When I do build one, I'd be opinionated about the structure. A coordinator with parallel workers rather than free-form agent-to-agent conversation, because open-ended chat between agents is where cost and confusion explode. Narrow structured interfaces between agents, passing typed results rather than prose, since prose handoffs are where information gets lost or hallucinated. Shared state kept external and authoritative rather than replicated in each agent's context, so agents don't diverge on facts. And hard caps on depth, iterations, and spend. Finally I'd design for partial failure explicitly, because the dangerous outcome isn't a crash, it's one worker silently failing and the coordinator confidently synthesizing an incomplete answer, so workers must report failure distinguishably from returning nothing.

cards.question: How do you prevent feedback loops from degrading a recommendation system over time?
options: Retrain more frequently on the most recent interaction data
Recognize that the model's own choices generate its training data, then counteract with exploration, logged propensities, off-policy correction, and diversity constraints
Freeze the model once it performs well
Use a larger model with more capacity
cards.explanation: Recommenders train on data produced by their own past recommendations, so the log is not a sample of user preference, it's a sample of what the system chose to show. Consequences: popularity concentration, since shown items get clicks and thus more exposure; filter bubbles narrowing each user's exposure; unshown items never accumulating evidence, so they can never be surfaced; and offline evaluation that flatters the incumbent because logged data is biased toward its choices. Retraining more often accelerates the loop rather than fixing it. Real countermeasures: deliberate exploration (epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, or a bandit formulation) so the log contains counterfactual information; logging propensities at serving time so you can apply inverse-propensity weighting or doubly-robust off-policy estimation; explicit diversity and novelty objectives or constraints in ranking; holding out a small randomized slice as an unbiased measurement channel; and monitoring catalog coverage and exposure distribution, not just engagement, since a system can look healthy on CTR while collapsing onto a shrinking item set.
cards.modelAnswer: The root problem is that a recommender's training data is generated by its own past decisions, so the interaction log isn't a sample of user preference, it's a sample of what the system chose to show and users happened to click. That creates several compounding effects: popularity concentration, because shown items get engagement which justifies showing them more; filter bubbles as each user's exposure narrows; and a structural blind spot where items never shown never accumulate evidence, so they can never earn exposure. It also corrupts measurement, since offline replay on logged data systematically favors the incumbent policy, which is why offline wins so often fail to reproduce online. I'd note that retraining more frequently makes this worse rather than better, because it tightens the loop. The countermeasures. Deliberate exploration, whether epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, or a full bandit formulation, so the log contains counterfactual information about items the greedy policy wouldn't have picked, and I'd frame the exploration cost as buying data rather than as lost revenue. Log propensities at serving time, which is a small engineering decision with large payoff, since without them you can't do inverse-propensity weighting or doubly-robust off-policy evaluation and you're stuck with biased offline estimates. Explicit diversity and novelty terms in the ranking objective or as constraints in a re-ranking stage, rather than hoping relevance produces variety. A small permanently randomized holdout slice as an unbiased measurement channel, which is expensive but is the only clean read on true preference. And monitoring the right things: catalog coverage, exposure concentration like a Gini coefficient over items, and long-term retention alongside CTR, because a system can look healthy on short-term engagement while collapsing onto a shrinking item set and slowly eroding both user and supplier satisfaction.

cards.question: Design an agent that takes actions in external systems. What safety architecture do you require?
options: A strong system prompt instructing the agent to be careful
Least-privilege scoped tools, human approval for irreversible actions, sandboxing, egress control, idempotency, spend and loop caps, and full audit logging
A safety classifier on the agent's output text
Restricting the agent to a single tool at a time
cards.explanation: The model is not a security boundary, so controls must be external and enforced in code. Required layers: tools scoped to least privilege and to the requesting user's own permissions, so a successful prompt injection can't escalate; read-write separation with human confirmation for anything irreversible, outward-facing, or high-value, including deletes, payments, and messages to third parties; sandboxed execution for generated code with no ambient credentials; egress allowlisting, since exfiltration needs an outbound channel and rendering a model-supplied URL is enough; idempotency keys and rate limits so retries don't double-charge or double-send; explicit loop, step, and spend caps because runaway agents are a cost and blast-radius problem; dry-run or plan-preview modes for high-stakes flows; and comprehensive audit logging of every action with its trigger so incidents can be reconstructed and reversed. Design assuming injection will sometimes succeed and ask whether untrusted content and sensitive capability need to be in the same session at all.
cards.modelAnswer: My starting principle is that the model is not a security boundary, so every control that matters is enforced in code outside it, and I'd design assuming prompt injection will sometimes succeed. Concretely, layers. Least privilege on tools, scoped to the requesting user's own permissions rather than a service account with broad rights, because if the agent can do more than the user, a successful injection is a privilege escalation. Read-write separation, with human confirmation required for anything irreversible, outward-facing, or high-value: deletes, payments, external messages, permission changes. That confirmation has to show the actual concrete action, not a summary the model wrote, since a model-authored description of its own action is exactly what an injection would manipulate. Sandboxed execution for any generated code, with no ambient credentials in the environment. Egress allowlisting, because exfiltration requires an outbound channel and people forget that rendering a model-supplied image URL or letting it fetch a link is sufficient to leak the entire context. Idempotency keys and rate limits on every mutating tool so a retry after a timeout doesn't double-charge or double-send. Hard caps on steps, loop depth, and spend per task, since a runaway agent is both a cost incident and an expanded blast radius. Dry-run or plan-preview modes for high-stakes workflows so a human sees the intended sequence before anything executes. And comprehensive audit logging of every action with the trigger that caused it, because after an incident you need to reconstruct and reverse what happened, and that's impossible without it. The architectural question I'd raise first, though, is whether untrusted content and sensitive capability need to be in the same session at all, because separating the agent that reads arbitrary web pages from the agent that can touch production data eliminates a whole class of attack rather than mitigating it.

cards.question: How would you design personalization without compromising privacy?
options: Anonymize user IDs and store all behavior data indefinitely
Minimize collection, prefer on-device or session-scoped signals, aggregate where possible, and use techniques like federated learning or differential privacy when individual data must inform models
Encrypt the user database and personalize freely
Require users to opt in, after which no further constraints apply
cards.explanation: Start from data minimization, since the strongest privacy protection is not collecting or retaining data you don't need, and much personalization value comes from session and context signals rather than long-term profiles. Prefer keeping sensitive signals on device with only aggregates or model updates leaving it, which is what federated learning formalizes, optionally with secure aggregation so the server sees only sums. Where individual data must train a shared model, differential privacy provides a quantifiable guarantee at a measurable utility cost, and you should be explicit about the epsilon rather than calling something private without one. Note that pseudonymization is weak, since behavioral data is highly re-identifiable, and that models memorize, so an LLM or embedding trained on user data can leak it, meaning embeddings should be treated as personal data since they're approximately invertible. Also design the operational side: purpose limitation, retention limits with real deletion including from indexes, caches, and logs, and genuine user controls with transparency about what is used, since regulation increasingly requires this and it's cheaper to build in than retrofit.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd start from data minimization, because the strongest guarantee is data you never collected, and I'd challenge the assumption that personalization requires a rich long-term profile. A great deal of value comes from session and context signals, what the user is doing right now, which are far less sensitive and often more predictive of immediate intent than a two-year history. Where I do need persistent signals, I'd prefer keeping them on the device and sending only aggregates or model updates, which is what federated learning formalizes, ideally with secure aggregation so the server sees only sums across many users rather than individual contributions. Where individual data must inform a shared model, differential privacy gives a quantifiable guarantee, and I'd insist on stating the epsilon and the utility cost explicitly, because calling a system private without a privacy parameter is marketing rather than engineering. Two technical points I'd raise that people miss. Pseudonymization is weak protection, since behavioral data is highly re-identifiable and a handful of interactions can uniquely fingerprint someone, so replacing a user ID with a hash isn't anonymization. And models memorize, so a model or embedding trained on user data can leak it, with embeddings in particular being approximately invertible, which means my vector store holds personal data and needs the same protection and deletion path as the source. Then the operational side, which is where most designs fail: purpose limitation so data collected for one feature isn't silently reused, retention limits with deletion that genuinely propagates to indexes, caches, and observability traces, and real user controls with plain-language transparency. I'd argue for building this in from the start rather than retrofitting, both because regulation increasingly requires it and because retrofitting deletion into a system that assumed permanent retention is far more expensive than designing for it.

cards.question: Your AI feature works well for the majority but poorly for a specific user segment. How do you address it?
options: Accept it, since aggregate metrics are strong
Diagnose the cause: data representation, distribution difference, or metric mismatch, then fix with targeted data, segment-aware modeling or thresholds, and per-segment monitoring
Train a completely separate model for that segment immediately
Exclude the segment from the feature to avoid poor experiences
cards.explanation: First diagnose, because the fix depends on the cause. Under-representation in training data calls for targeted collection or reweighting. A genuinely different input distribution (another language, different device, different usage pattern) may need features or preprocessing that generalize, or a segment-specific model. A metric or threshold mismatch means the model may rank fine for that segment but a globally-tuned threshold is wrong for its base rate, in which case per-segment calibration fixes it cheaply. Sometimes the label definition itself doesn't transfer, which is the hardest case and requires rethinking the target. Then fix with the least complex sufficient intervention, preferring shared models with segment-aware features or calibration over separate models, since every extra model multiplies maintenance and can drift independently. Critically, add per-segment metrics to standing dashboards and release gates so the disparity can't reappear silently, since this happened in the first place because only aggregates were being watched. Also weigh whether the disparity has fairness or legal implications, which changes the urgency and who needs to be involved.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd diagnose before fixing, because there are several distinct causes and they need different interventions. Under-representation in training data is the most common: the segment is a small share of the data so the model optimizes for the majority, and the fix is targeted collection or reweighting. A genuinely different input distribution is next, another language, different devices, different usage patterns, where the model isn't biased so much as being asked something it hasn't seen, and the fix is features or preprocessing that generalize, or a segment-specific component. Third and often overlooked, a threshold or calibration mismatch: the model may rank perfectly well for that segment while a globally tuned threshold is wrong for its base rate, and per-segment calibration fixes that cheaply without touching the model. Fourth and hardest, the label definition doesn't transfer, meaning what counts as a good outcome genuinely differs for that segment, which requires rethinking the target rather than the model. Then I'd apply the least complex sufficient fix, and I'd resist jumping to a separate model, because every additional model multiplies maintenance, drifts independently, and creates a segment that quietly stops being monitored, so I'd prefer one model with segment-aware features or calibration unless that demonstrably can't work. The structural fix matters as much as the immediate one: per-segment metrics go into standing dashboards and into release gates, because the reason this surfaced late is that only aggregates were being watched, and without that change the next disparity will also be found by a user rather than by us. And I'd assess whether the affected segment correlates with a protected characteristic, since that changes this from a quality issue into a fairness and potentially legal one, with different urgency and different people who need to be in the room.

cards.question: Design a real-time content ranking system for a feed with a strict latency budget. Where does the time go?
options: Almost entirely in model inference, so use the smallest model possible
Distributed across candidate retrieval, feature fetching, model scoring, and re-ranking, with feature fetching and fan-out often dominating rather than the model
In network transfer of the response payload
In the database write of impression logs
cards.explanation: Latency is usually spread across stages, and feature fetching is commonly the largest and most variable component, since scoring hundreds of candidates means fetching user, item, and cross features from multiple stores, so batched lookups, colocation, caching, and tail-latency control matter more than shaving model FLOPs. Candidate retrieval fans out to several sources in parallel, so its cost is the slowest source plus fusion, which argues for per-source timeouts and partial-result tolerance rather than waiting for all. Model scoring is often modest for a well-sized ranker on a batch of candidates, though it grows with candidate count and feature width. Re-ranking for diversity and business rules is usually cheap but sequential. Design implications: parallelize aggressively, precompute what you can (embeddings, item features, cached candidate pools), degrade gracefully by dropping optional stages under load rather than breaching the SLO, and budget explicitly at p99, since a feed request fans out to many dependencies and the slowest one determines the user's experience.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd resist the assumption that the model dominates, because in most feed systems it doesn't. The time is distributed, and feature fetching is frequently the largest and most variable slice: scoring several hundred candidates means assembling user features, per-item features, and cross features from multiple stores, so you're doing fan-out reads under a tight budget, and that means batched multi-get rather than per-candidate lookups, colocating or caching hot features, and controlling tail latency, since with hundreds of reads per request your p99 is determined by the slowest read almost every time. Candidate retrieval fans out to several sources in parallel, ANN over embeddings plus trending plus follow-graph plus recency, so its cost is the slowest source plus fusion, which is why I'd put per-source timeouts on it and tolerate partial results rather than blocking on the laggard. Model scoring for a right-sized ranker over a batched candidate set is often a modest share, though it scales with candidate count and feature width, so the real lever there is candidate count, not architecture. Re-ranking for diversity, dedup, and business rules is usually cheap but inherently sequential. So the design implications are: parallelize everything independent, precompute aggressively, item embeddings and features, and cached candidate pools per user refreshed asynchronously, so the online path assembles rather than computes. Then degrade gracefully under load, dropping optional sources or skipping reranking rather than breaching the SLO, and make that a designed behavior with monitoring rather than an accident. And I'd budget explicitly at p99 rather than the mean, because a feed request touches many dependencies and mean latency systematically understates what users experience.

cards.question: How do you migrate a rule-based system to ML without a risky big-bang cutover?
options: Replace the rules with the model on a chosen date after offline validation
Run the model in shadow against the rules, compare disagreements with human adjudication, then take over incrementally by segment or confidence band while keeping rules as fallback
Delete the rules first so the model isn't constrained by legacy logic
Have the model learn to reproduce the rules exactly, then extend it
cards.explanation: The rules encode real institutional knowledge, including edge cases nobody documented, so treating them as legacy to discard loses information and trust. A safer path: use rule outputs and historical decisions as an initial label source and baseline, run the model in shadow mode on live traffic, and focus on the disagreements, since those are where the information is, having humans adjudicate a sample to learn whether the model or the rule is right. That adjudication both measures readiness and produces high-value training labels. Then take over incrementally, by segment, by confidence band, or by percentage of traffic, with rules retained as a fallback and as guardrails for cases where a hard constraint is genuinely required, since some rules encode policy or legal requirements that shouldn't be probabilistic. Keep the ability to explain decisions during transition, since stakeholders who trusted transparent rules need equivalent confidence in the model, and monitor per-segment so a global improvement isn't hiding a regression on a case the rules handled well.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd start by respecting the rules rather than treating them as legacy to be swept away, because they encode years of institutional knowledge including edge cases nobody wrote down, and the fastest way to lose stakeholder trust is to regress on a case the old system handled correctly. Practically, the rules also give me two things immediately: a baseline to beat and an initial label source from historical decisions and their outcomes. Then shadow mode: run the model on live traffic alongside the rules without acting on its output, which costs nothing and validates the mechanics against the real input distribution. The valuable part is the disagreements, because that's where all the information is, so I'd sample them and have domain experts adjudicate who was right. That does double duty, measuring readiness in a way stakeholders find credible and producing high-value training labels precisely where the model is weak. Then incremental takeover rather than a cutover: by segment, by confidence band, or by traffic percentage, with rules retained as fallback. I'd also be explicit that some rules should stay permanently rather than being absorbed, because a rule that encodes a legal requirement or a hard policy constraint shouldn't become probabilistic, so the end state is usually a model with a rules layer for hard constraints rather than a pure model. Two things I'd manage alongside the technical work: explainability during transition, since people who trusted a transparent rule need comparable confidence in a model decision, and per-segment monitoring, because an aggregate improvement can easily conceal a regression on a narrow case the rules handled well, and that's exactly the regression that generates the loudest objections and can stall the whole migration.

cards.question: How do you design an evaluation and rollout strategy for a generative feature where quality is subjective?
options: Ship it and rely on user complaints as the quality signal
Define quality dimensions with stakeholders, use pairwise comparison and validated judges offline, then stage rollout with behavioral proxies and guardrails online
Use BLEU against reference outputs written by the product team
Have the model rate its own outputs and gate on that score
cards.explanation: Subjective doesn't mean unmeasurable, but it does mean you must decompose it. Work with stakeholders to name the dimensions that matter (factual accuracy, tone fit, usefulness, format compliance, safety) and rate them separately, since a single overall score conflates things that need different fixes. Offline, prefer pairwise comparison over absolute scoring because humans and LLM judges are both far more reliable at relative judgments, and validate any LLM judge against human labels before trusting it, controlling for position and verbosity bias. Online, subjective quality shows up in behavior rather than ratings, so instrument implicit signals such as acceptance and edit rates, regeneration and retry rates, copy or share actions, and abandonment, which are abundant compared with explicit thumbs. Stage the rollout: internal use, then a small cohort, then expansion, with guardrails on safety, latency, and cost that block regardless of quality gains. Throughout, feed real failures into the offline set so it converges on production reality, and accept that the goal is detecting regressions and large improvements reliably rather than resolving small differences precisely.
cards.modelAnswer: Subjective doesn't mean unmeasurable, it means I have to decompose it before I can measure it. So first, with stakeholders, name the dimensions that actually matter, factual accuracy, tone and brand fit, usefulness, format compliance, safety, and rate them separately, because a single overall score conflates dimensions that need different fixes and hides which one regressed. Writing that rubric usually surfaces genuine disagreement among stakeholders, which is much cheaper to resolve before launch. Offline, I'd use pairwise comparison rather than absolute scoring, since both humans and LLM judges are substantially more reliable at saying A is better than B than at assigning a seven out of ten, and absolute scales drift between sessions. If I use an LLM judge for scale, I'd validate its agreement against human labels first and control for position and verbosity bias by swapping orders and averaging, because an unvalidated judge just relocates the trust problem. Online is where subjective quality actually reveals itself, and it shows up in behavior rather than ratings: acceptance and edit rates, how much users modify what was generated, regeneration and retry rates, copy or share actions, and abandonment. Those are far more abundant and less biased than explicit thumbs, which only a self-selecting minority ever click. Rollout would be staged: internal dogfooding first, which catches an enormous amount cheaply, then a small cohort, then expansion, with guardrails on safety, latency, and cost that block promotion regardless of how good the quality numbers look. And throughout, every real failure goes into the offline set so it converges toward production reality. The expectation I'd set explicitly is that the goal is reliably detecting regressions and large improvements, not resolving two-percent differences precisely, because with subjective quality the measurement noise floor is real and pretending otherwise leads to shipping on noise.

cards.question: You're asked to add an AI feature that you believe won't work well. How do you handle it?
options: Refuse to build it and explain that the technology isn't ready
State the specific concern and its evidence, propose a cheap experiment or narrower scope that tests the risky assumption, and build the full thing if the decision stands
Build it as specified without comment, since scope is the requester's call
Build a deliberately limited version to demonstrate the problem
cards.explanation: The professional move is neither silent compliance nor refusal. Name the concern concretely, with the specific failure mode and the evidence for it, rather than a general appeal to difficulty, because a vague objection is easy to dismiss and hard to act on. Then propose a way to resolve the disagreement empirically and cheaply: a small evaluation set that measures the risky assumption in days, a prototype on the hardest cases rather than the easiest, or a narrower initial scope that delivers value while testing feasibility. That reframes it from opinion versus opinion into a question with an answer, which is usually what unblocks the conversation. Also distinguish the type of risk, since a quality concern is a tradeoff the business can legitimately accept, while a safety, privacy, legal, or reputational risk needs escalation and explicit sign-off rather than quiet acceptance. If the decision stands after that, build it properly and instrument it well, because a half-hearted implementation makes the outcome uninterpretable, and note the assumptions in writing so the eventual result is a shared learning rather than an argument about who was right.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd neither refuse nor comply silently. First I'd make the concern specific and evidence-based, naming the concrete failure mode, this needs multi-step arithmetic and current models are unreliable there, or this requires facts that change daily and our retrieval latency budget can't support it, rather than a general appeal to it being hard, because a vague objection is easy to dismiss and gives the requester nothing to act on. Then I'd try to convert the disagreement into an experiment, which is usually what actually unblocks the conversation: build a fifty-case evaluation set and measure the risky assumption in a few days, or prototype against the hardest cases rather than the demo-friendly ones, since a demo built on easy examples is exactly how these projects get committed to. Often a narrower initial scope both delivers real value and tests feasibility, so I'd propose that. I'd also distinguish what kind of risk I'm raising, because that determines who decides. A quality or ROI concern is a legitimate business tradeoff, and if the product owner hears my evidence and still wants it, that's their call and I'd say so plainly. A safety, privacy, legal, or reputational risk is different, and that needs explicit escalation and sign-off rather than my quiet acquiescence, because accepting that risk isn't mine to accept alone. If the decision stands, I'd build it properly and instrument it well, since a half-hearted implementation makes the result uninterpretable and I'd have no idea whether my concern was right or my execution was bad. And I'd write down the assumption and the expected failure mode up front, so when we get data it's a shared learning about the problem rather than a retrospective argument about who was right, which is both more useful and considerably better for the working relationship.

cards.question: How would you design a system that must work reliably in multiple languages?
options: Translate everything to English, process, and translate back
Evaluate per language rather than in aggregate, choose multilingual models and tokenizers deliberately, and design fallbacks by language tier since quality will be uneven
Train a separate model per language from scratch
Use a single large model, since modern LLMs handle all languages equally
cards.explanation: Quality is genuinely uneven across languages because pretraining data is, so the first requirement is measuring per language rather than reporting an average that hides which languages are unusable. Tokenization matters materially: non-Latin scripts and morphologically rich languages consume several times more tokens for the same content, which raises cost, consumes context, and can degrade quality, so tokenizer efficiency is a real selection criterion. Translate-to-English is a legitimate pattern for some pipelines but it compounds errors, loses nuance and named entities, and adds latency, so it's a fallback rather than a default. For retrieval, decide between multilingual embeddings, which enable cross-lingual matching, and per-language indexes, which often retrieve better within a language, and remember that a query in one language may need documents in another. Then design by tier: full support with evaluation and human review for primary languages, best-effort with monitoring for secondary ones, and explicit graceful degradation rather than silent poor quality for the rest. Also account for locale-specific facts, formats, and cultural context, and for right-to-left rendering and text expansion on the UI side.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd start from the honest premise that quality will be uneven, because pretraining data is uneven, so the first design requirement is measuring per language instead of reporting an aggregate that averages a great English experience with an unusable Vietnamese one. That means per-language eval sets with native-speaker labeling for the languages I claim to support, which is a real cost I'd budget rather than discover. Tokenization is a concrete issue people miss: non-Latin scripts and morphologically rich languages often consume two to four times more tokens for equivalent content, which directly raises cost, eats context window, and correlates with worse quality, so tokenizer efficiency across my target languages becomes a genuine model selection criterion, not a footnote. On architecture, translate-to-English-and-back is a legitimate pattern and sometimes the pragmatic answer, but it compounds errors across three steps, mangles named entities and domain terms, loses nuance and register, and adds latency, so I'd treat it as a fallback for long-tail languages rather than the default path. For retrieval, I'd decide deliberately between multilingual embeddings, which let a query in one language match documents in another and are essential if my content is primarily in one language, versus per-language indexes, which typically retrieve better within a language, and I'd test rather than assume. Then I'd design in tiers: primary languages get full evaluation, tuned prompts, and human review; secondary get best-effort with monitoring; the rest get explicit graceful degradation, and I'd argue for telling the user this feature works best in these languages rather than silently serving bad output, since silent poor quality erodes trust worse than an honest limitation. And I'd cover the non-model parts, locale-specific facts and formats, cultural context in generated content, right-to-left rendering, and UI text expansion, since those are where multilingual products visibly break even when the model is fine.

cards.question: You have three months to add AI to an existing product with no ML infrastructure. What do you prioritize?
options: Build the platform first: feature store, training pipelines, and model registry
Pick one high-value narrow use case, ship it end to end with hosted APIs and an evaluation harness, then build infrastructure driven by real needs
Hire an ML team before writing any code
Fine-tune a model on the company's data to establish a differentiated asset
cards.explanation: Platform-first is a common and expensive mistake, because you end up building abstractions for requirements you don't understand yet, and after three months you have infrastructure and no shipped value. Instead pick one use case that is genuinely valuable, narrow enough to finish, and tolerant of errors, then ship it end to end: hosted APIs to avoid owning serving, retrieval for knowledge rather than fine-tuning, and a small evaluation harness plus tracing from day one, since those are the two investments that keep paying and are painful to retrofit. Shipping teaches you what your actual data problems, latency constraints, and failure modes are, and that knowledge is what should determine which infrastructure you build second. Also plan the organizational side: instrument feedback capture, set expectations that the first version will be imperfect and improved iteratively, and choose a use case with a measurable outcome so you can demonstrate value and earn budget for the next step. Fine-tuning early is usually premature, since you don't yet have the data or the evaluation to know whether it helps.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd pick one narrow high-value use case and ship it end to end, and explicitly not build a platform first, because platform-first means designing abstractions for requirements I don't understand yet and arriving at month three with infrastructure and nothing shipped, which also costs me the credibility needed to fund the next phase. Selection criteria for that first use case: genuinely valuable so success is visible, narrow enough to finish in the window, and tolerant of imperfection, so I'd prefer an internal or assistive feature over an automated customer-facing decision, since the blast radius of early mistakes is what kills these programs. Then I'd deliberately minimize what I own: hosted APIs rather than self-hosted serving, retrieval for knowledge rather than fine-tuning, and off-the-shelf components wherever possible, because owning GPU capacity and training pipelines in month one is buying problems I don't have yet. The two things I would invest in properly from day one are an evaluation harness and tracing, because they're what make every subsequent iteration measurable rather than guesswork, and both are genuinely painful to retrofit once there's traffic. Shipping is also how I learn what infrastructure I actually need: after one real feature I'll know where my data is broken, what my latency budget truly is, and which failure modes matter, and that should drive what I build second rather than a generic reference architecture. On the organizational side I'd instrument feedback capture from launch, set the expectation explicitly that version one is a starting point to be improved with real data rather than a finished product, and choose something with a measurable outcome so I can demonstrate value and earn the mandate for the next step. And I'd defer fine-tuning, since without data and evaluation I can't even tell whether it would help, and it's the classic way to spend two of the three months on something unfalsifiable.
